Jimmy Rogers  Iowa State
Time will tell whether or not this is a good hire, but AD Jamie Pollard has made some good ones with Matt Campbell on 
the football side and Fred Hoiberg, Steve Prohm, and T.J. Otzelberger on the basketball side. He spent $4 million to buy 
Rogers out of his Washington State contract, so he was locked in from the jump on the 39-year-old, who won the FCS 
National Championship in his first season as a head coach at South Dakota State and lost in the semifinal in Year 2. This 
will be just his third year at the FBS level, having served as a GA at Florida Atlantic in 2012 under Carl Pelini and then as 
the head coach of Wazzu last season. Pollard unequivocally deserves the benefit of the doubt here and Rogers is inheriting 
a much better foundation than his predecessor did from Paul Rhoads.
Collin Klein  Kansas State
After spreading his wings to fly to College Station for two seasons, Klein is back in the Little Apple to coach at his alma 
mater. Klein was on the staff in 2014-15 and again from 2017-23, serving primarily as the QB coach and then OC. He’s 
one of the best players in the program’s history and he does seem to be a solid coach, given that he’s only 36 and already 
has this job after Chris Klieman and Bill Snyder, two guys who excelled in Manhattan for boosters and bettors. With OC 
Sean Gleeson and DC Jordan Peterson, this is a young staff that will learn and grow together, so bumps in the road are 
inevitable and this was just a 6-6 program last season.
Eric Morris  Oklahoma State
A return to the glory days of Oklahoma State football may not be that far away. It is hard to believe that this was a top-
10 team in 2021 and a 10-win team in 2023 with just how badly it has gone the last two seasons. The Cowboys were a 
combined 4-20, prompting the pink slip for longtime head coach Mike “Teach Me How To” Gundy. That included an 0-18 
record in the new-look Big 12. Enter Eric Morris, who played and coached under Mike Leach and Kliff Kingsbury, and 
who led North Texas to the program’s first AP ranking in over 65 years and a chance at being the G5 CFP representative. 
The gunslinger mentality is back in Stillwater and I think the Cowboys make a big leap, especially with an excellent DC in 
Skyler Cassity.
Morgan Scalley  Utah
After basically a decade of being the head coach-in-waiting, except for a short period of time after a scandal involving 
the use of racial stereotypes, Scalley gets his shot with Whittingham off to Michigan. Scalley coached the Utes in the Las 
Vegas Bowl to a 44-22 win and now he’s the full-time guy. The Salt Lake City native played at Utah and has coached at 
Utah since 2007, serving as DC for the last 10 seasons. He certainly knows the program and is plenty familiar with the 
recruiting pipelines. It may work out, though Year 3 in the Big 12 might be a little bit rocky.
BIG  12
Morgan Scalley

Kyle Whittingham  Michigan
Sherrone Moore’s ugly departure from Ann Arbor on the heels of Jim Harbaugh’s tainted National Championship 
created the need for a well-respected, accomplished football lifer to clean up the program. Enter Whittingham, who 
calls somewhere other than Salt Lake City home for the first time since he was the DC at Idaho State from 1992-93. I’ll 
be honest - Whittingham has long been viewed as one of the game’s elite coaches, both against the spread and in terms 
of maximizing talent. His Utah teams were always tough to face because of their presence in the trenches. But, I am 
skeptical of the 66-year-old entering the Big Ten and a program with extreme expectations.
Pat Fitzgerald  Michigan State
It might be unfair to call a College Football Hall of Famer an underwhelming hire, but this is an underwhelming hire. 
Fitzgerald was dismissed from Northwestern in 2023 following an investigation into hazing and sexual assault. A thorough 
investigation was completed and Fitzgerald was shown the door, though it’s hard not to wonder if he would have had more 
program support if the team hadn’t gone 1-11 the previous season and 3-9 the season before that. Either way, Fitzgerald, 
who was a volunteer coach at his son’s high school for the last three seasons, gets another chance after the aspirational 
hire of Jonathan Smith didn’t work out. It feels like the ceiling in East Lansing is very low moving forward.
Matt Campbell  Penn State
Of all the Power Four hires, this is the hardest one to project in my estimation. After a decade at Iowa State, where 
Campbell really built up the Cyclones amid a lot of financial and reputational shortcomings in a high-octane offensive 
conference, Penn State is a different beast. Campbell’s four-year run at Toledo was great and his decade in Ames was 
tremendous, but this is a BIG job. Campbell has strong Ohio ties, which should help with recruiting and he did really well 
to get D’Anton Lynn, a Texas native, as the DC, giving Penn State a lot of connections from coast to coast. What stood out 
at Iowa State is how Campbell maximized the talent he was able to recruit. With more fertile recruiting grounds now, 
what can he do with more talent? That’ll be the big question, and maybe one not quite answered in 2026.
Bob Chesney  UCLA
The hire of former James Madison head coach Curt Cignetti seemed to work out at Indiana, and now the Bruins’ athletic 
department is hoping for the same with Chesney, who was at Holy Cross prior to his two seasons with the Dukes. Chesney 
is a winner with a career 132-52 record and he took JMU to the College Football Playoff as the G5 representative last 
season. For a Bruins bunch that has only finished the season ranked one time since 2014, the bar isn’t terribly high, 
so Chesney, a strong hire by all accounts, has the chance to rapidly improve the program, even with a tough Big Ten 
schedule.
BIG  TEN

Casey Woods  Missouri State
Missouri State had to be quietly planning for Ryan Beard to be offered another job, but they probably didn’t think it would 
be so soon. With Beard off to Coastal Carolina following the program’s first FBS season, AD Patrick Ransdell, who got the 
job just before the start of the football season, moved quickly to hire Woods from SMU. Woods has worn a lot of different

football, having worked at App State and UCF previously, so I think he’s trustworthy in isolating Woods as quickly as

coaching vet Sparky Woods, probably ends up being a solid hire.
Alex Mortensen  UAB
Mortensen isn’t a new head coach, per se, as he took over when Trent Dilfer was booted from Birmingham, but he’s the

very well have been the deciding factor in just keeping him. The Dilfer hire was out of left field, to say the least, when the 
players desperately wanted Bryant Vincent to take over the job permanently when he filled in for Bill Clark, but that didn’t 
happen. Simply elevating Mortensen from OC reeks of being too cheap to make an impact hire.
Jason Candle  UConn
On the surface, this looks like a great hire. Candle went 81-44 at Toledo and had no problems succeeding Matt Campbell 
with the newfound success he brought to the Rockets. At the same time, Campbell only won the MAC twice in 10 seasons 
as the head coach and owns a career bowl record of 3-5. Not to mention, the Rockets have had a penchant for losing 
games as a big favorite, losing more than 10 times as a TD+ favorite from 2021-25. On the plus side, he won’t see a lot of 
big favorite roles with the Huskies. On the downside, a program like UConn simply has to win games in which they are 
favored and Candle has had major problems doing just that.

Mark Carney  Kent State
Anybody who wins five games at Kent State deserves Coach of the Year consideration. For Carney, starting the season 3-5

John Hauser  Ohio
“New” head coach is a loose term here, as Hauser was the assistant head coach and DC for the Bobcats before HC Brian

Alonzo Carter  Sacramento State
Two things first… Yes, Sacramento State is an FBS team now. And, yes, they are in the MAC. Carter is a Brent Brennan

the basketball team with head coach Mike Bibby and GM Shaquille O’Neal, Carter, a one-time backup dancer for MC

Mike Jacobs  Toledo
Jacobs, a Maumee native from northwestern Ohio, worked his way up the hard way, serving as the head coach at Division 
II Notre Dame College (OH) and Lenoir-Rhyne before getting an opportunity in the FCS ranks at Mercer. It is kind of 
rare to see a head coach with this sort of path, as many have been coordinators or position coaches at the FBS level, and 
usually from a P4 school at some point. Jacobs is 94-23 in his career as a head coach and took Mercer to the FCS Playoffs 
in back-to-back seasons. Mercer had one of the nation’s best defenses in 2024 and the offense racked up nearly 500 yards 
per game in 2025. Given Candle’s inability to do what needs to be done as a favorite, this could end up being quite the 
upgrade.

Rob Harley  Northern Illinois
If Sacramento State being in the MAC wasn’t enough of a mind-eff, Northern Illinois is a member of the retooled

Jim Mora  Colorado State
Let’s all take a second and come to terms with the fact that Colorado State is now in the Pac-12…Alright, now let’s think

JaMarcus Shephard  Oregon State
Going the defensive route didn’t work, so Oregon State has gone in the other direction. Tyler Bray really walked into

assistant head coach and now is a head coach looking to install a dramatically different offense.
Kirby Moore  Washington State
Moore, whose time at Boise State crossed over with brother Kellen, who has a slightly more high-profile job, is on the fast 
track. The 35-year-old isn’t coaching the Saints like his 37-year-old brother, but three years of calling plays at Missouri 
and one at Fresno State now has him in a head coaching role. Grabbing a branch of the Chris Petersen, Kalen DeBoer, 
Eli Drinkwitz coaching tree is far from a bad idea, but he’s going to need to grow into the role with a program that hasn’t 
really been investing in its roster while being a Pac-12 orphan with Mountain West guardianship. Now back in the Pac-12, 
the program will invest in the head coach and the roster all at once and that will probably take some time.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
Ryan Silverfield  Arkansas
After a decade at Memphis, Silverfield packed up the family and took I-40 to I-49 for probably the only SEC opportunity 
he was ever going to get. It would be unfair to call him the last person at the bar when the “ugly lights” came on, but AD 
Hunter Yurachek had two strikes in the count and had to put a ball in play. Silverfield was seemingly the bronze medalist 
behind Jon Sumrall and Alex Golesh, and you can see why. He inherited a good program and a NIL budget filled by FedEx 
at Memphis and never won the conference. The irony is not lost on me that the Razorbacks went from an OL coach in 
Sam Pittman to another OL coach in Silverfield, as they look to finish the season ranked for just the second time since 
2011.
Alex Golesh  Auburn
You can see what Auburn was thinking here, as the Tigers have scored just 18.5 and 19.1 PPG against SEC opponents 
over the last two seasons. Golesh is an offensive guy through and through, spending his entire collegiate coaching career 
on that side of the ball. After four seasons under Matt Campbell and three under Josh Heupel, Golesh got his first HC 
opportunity at South Florida and went 23-15 before taking the Auburn gig. Given that the defense is in the hands of 
veterans D.J. Durkin and Tim Banks, Golesh’s chief objective is to find points and he’s done that pretty much everywhere 
he’s been. His first-year success will be contingent on how the USF transfers adapt to P4 life, including QB Byrum Brown.
Jon Sumrall  Florida
Sumrall’s trajectory is becoming increasingly common in college football. The 43-year-old played four years at Kentucky, 
where he then served as a grad assistant from 2005-06 before getting a FCS gig at San Diego in his mid-20s. From there, he 
moved up the ranks, eventually serving as the co-DC at Kentucky before two seasons as the head coach at Troy and two at 
Tulane. Having immediate success adds commas to your bank account in CFB and that’s the case for Sumrall, who made 
the CFP with Tulane in 2024 and has won at least 11 games in three of his four seasons as a HC. While he inherited a mess 
at Troy from Chip Lindsey, he inherited a strong foundation at Tulane thanks to Willie Fritz. Florida, one of the sport’s 
premier programs, could be classified as somewhere in between, so we’ll see how long it takes Sumrall to bring them 
back to relevance.
Will Stein  Kentucky
Personally, I really like this hire, especially when paired with a strong DC grab in Jay Bateman. Stein, the mastermind of 
the Oregon offense the last three seasons, is a Louisville native and played QB there from 2008-12. Props to the Kentucky 
athletic department for realizing that the program needs to modernize offensively. What Mark Stoops did, including eight 
straight bowl game appearances from 2016-23, was very impressive with the team’s tenacious defense and ball-control 
offense, but for Kentucky to take the leap into being a legitimate contender, a more dynamic offense will be required, 
especially in the SEC. Former Dan Lanning OC Kenny Dillingham has done pretty well at Arizona State, but the Sun Devils 
were 3-9 in his first season as he tore the team down to the studs. Something to keep in mind with Stein.
Lane Kiffin  LSU
The Lane Train made a lot of noise leaving Oxford for Baton Rouge, as he bailed on his College Football Playoff squad to 
set things in motion with the Tigers. There are a lot of must-see games during the CFB season - it’s possible that none of 
them will top September 19, when LSU visits Ole Miss. Lane is one of the most recognizable cast members in the college 
football soap opera, but he’s also a guy who recruited at an obscene level and led a collective 32-6 run over his final three 
seasons with the Rebels. Does his move to LSU conjure up memories of his ill-fated stint at USC? Probably, based on 
the blue blood running through the veins of both institutions. But we cannot argue that Kiffin plays an exciting style of 
football and gets dudes who can ball out on both sides. Just what LSU needs.
Pete Golding  Mississippi
This was a tough situation for AD Keith Carter. The players rallied around Golding amidst the made-for-TV drama of Lane 
Kiffin’s exit. At the same time, with Kiffin’s offensive reputation and penchant for recruiting, including the JUCO ranks, it 
is hard not to feel underwhelmed about Golding. That said, the Rebels played extremely well in the CFP, beating Tulane 
and Georgia before falling short to Miami. Golding has also worked under now-Browns head coach Todd Monken at 
Southern Miss, new Arkansas DC Ron Roberts at SE Louisiana, Frank Wilson at UTSA, Nick Saban at Alabama, and Kiffin.

Ryan Beard  Coastal Carolina
After overseeing Missouri State’s transition from FCS to FBS, Beard took the Bears to a bowl game in their first season

Billy Napier  James Madison

Blake Anderson  Southern Miss

both stops and has done so while navigating some very difficult and tragic family circumstances, so we’ll see how this stop 
goes.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
If the Curt Cignetti story was a Disney movie, it would be mocked as 
absurd and completely unrealistic. A coach who waited several years 
for his first big shot finally gets it with the losingest program in college 
football history, and Indiana goes 16-0 to win the national championship 
in his second season.
“Hoosiers” was a classic movie based on a true high school basketball 
Cinderella story in the 1950s, and Cignetti basically scripted the 
sequel.
“What if I told you at the end of the 2023 season that Indiana would 
have an undefeated national champion in two years? There’s no chance 
anyone would have believed me,” DraftKings oddsmaker Matt Grill said. 
“You would say there’s absolutely no way in hell that could happen. It 
was a forgotten program. I still don’t know how he did it.”
Indiana lost its 2023 season finale at Purdue to finish 3-9. In their history, 
the Hoosiers never had a 10-win season and owned only three bowl 
wins. In two years in Bloomington, Cignetti has a 27-2 record. Last year, 
he upset Ohio State to win the Big Ten championship before blowing out 
Alabama in the Rose Bowl and Oregon in the Peach Bowl on the way to a 
victory over Miami for the national title.
“Cignetti is amazing,” Grill said. “I think Indiana is going to keep it 
going, but pretty much no one is betting Indiana.”
Ohio State, Notre Dame and Texas are attracting a majority of the 
affection as college football futures action heats up in Nevada and across 
the country. In their bid for a repeat, the Hoosiers are getting a cold 
shoulder from the betting public at most books. Indiana is posted at 10-1 
odds as the fifth choice on the board at Circa Sports.
“Texas is currently the favorite to win the title, though it didn’t open 
that way, and it’s because we’ve taken sharp action on them,” Circa vice 
president of operations Mike Palm said. “We took our sharpest limit bet 
on Texas at +750.”
The limit bet on Longhorns was for $10,000, Palm said. Texas is the +650 
favorites at Circa, followed by Ohio State (+700), Notre Dame (+725), 
Oregon (+730) and Georgia (+950).
“We’ve seen a ton of public interest in Notre Dame and Oregon — those 
are our two biggest realistic liabilities,” Palm said.
Boomer’s Sportsbook director Nick Bogdanovich said the public is 
“betting Notre Dame with both hands,” driving the Fighting Irish from 
8-1 to 6-1 odds.
Notre Dame started last season 0-2, losing games to Miami and Texas 
A&M by a total of four points, and finished 10-2. The Irish were 
controversially excluded from the 12-team College Football Playoff and 
are expected to stage a revenge tour behind coach Marcus Freeman and 
a veteran team headlined by sophomore quarterback CJ Carr.
“Notre Dame should be able to navigate this schedule to an undefeated 
regular season,” Palm said. “Whether the Irish are good enough to beat 
Texas and Ohio State is a different question.”
Two years ago, the Irish eliminated Indiana and Cignetti in the first 
round of the CFP and fell to Ohio State in the national title game. The 
Buckeyes are currently the +600 favorites at DraftKings, ahead of Notre 
Dame at +650.
“We took a lot of money on Notre Dame early when we opened 10-1,” 
Grill said. “I’ve got Ohio State as my No. 1 team right now.”
Grill’s power ratings show Notre Dame and Indiana tied at No. 2, 
followed by Oregon, Georgia, Texas, Texas Tech, Miami, Texas A&M and 
Alabama. Grill said he’s not sold on the Longhorns and quarterback Arch 
Manning, who was overhyped entering last season.
“I’m sure I’ve got a similar Top 10 to about everyone else out there,” Grill 
said. “The potential is there with Texas. It’s an embarrassment of riches. 
If Arch is improved and slinging it, they could be phenomenal. But Texas 
disappoints every year for how long now?”
Texas hosts Ohio State on Sept. 12 in one of the season’s most pivotal 
games. Manning was a bust in the teams’ season opener a year ago, 
when the Buckeyes won 14-7. In addition to the game at Texas, the 
Buckeyes will face road tests against Indiana, Iowa and USC as part of a 
grueling schedule.
“My top three teams are Ohio State, Oregon and Notre Dame,” South 
Point sportsbook director Chris Andrews said. “I know we have action 
on those three, plus USC.”
With coach Lincoln Riley under pressure entering his fifth year, the 
Trojans are 35-1 longshots at DraftKings. USC hosts Oregon in late 
September, hosts Ohio State in late October and plays at Indiana on Nov. 
14.
Aside from Cignetti, the coach who’s probably talked about the most in 
the media is Lane Kiffin, who ditched Mississippi prior to the CFP and 
took the LSU job. The Tigers are a 16-1 shot at Circa.
“We’ve seen sharp interest in LSU, and USC has been bet from 50-1 down 
to 30-1,” Palm said.
Not everyone believes in and roots for Kiffin, of course, and his childish 
diva act gets annoying. The most action the Boomer’s book has seen 
in the Yes/No playoff market, Bogdanovich said, is on LSU to miss the 
playoffs at -125.
Texas and Georgia are the SEC’s best bets to break the Big Ten’s three-
year championship reign strung together by Michigan, Ohio State 
and Indiana. The Hoosiers must replace Heisman Trophy-winning 
quarterback Fernando Mendoza, and the Heisman market is generating 
action all over the board with a surplus of marquee QBs this season. At 
DraftKings, Carr is the Heisman favorite at +700 and Manning is the +800 
second choice.
“The expanded playoff certainly creates more futures action in Yes/No 
playoffs as well as to win the national championship,” Palm said. “The 
expansion to 12 teams tripled the handle in those markets. I don’t want 
to see more than 16 teams. I actually think 12 is a very practical number, 
and beyond 16 will include too many teams with no chance of winning 
the title.”
Not long ago, before Cignetti showed up and changed everything, 
Indiana seemed to be a team with no shot of winning a championship.
nobody believed then.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
The recent history of the Heisman Trophy suggests it’s become 
a quarterback’s award. Travis Hunter, a rare two-way superstar, 
broke the mold in 2024, but he’s the exception — only five non-
quarterbacks have won since 2000. That trend has only intensified 
since college football’s NIL era officially kicked off in July 2021. 
Since NIL money started flowing openly, four of the last five 
winners have been quarterbacks.
There’s a newer wrinkle worth watching, though: three of the 
last four winners have been hired guns. Caleb Williams, Jayden 
Daniels, and Fernando Mendoza all won after transferring in 
from other power programs, and that’s a pattern to keep in mind 
entering the 2026 season.
One more thing to file away: the preseason betting favorite rarely 
actually wins. Depending on the book, CJ Carr and Arch Manning 
currently top the oddsboard. Both enter the new season with 
outrageous hype, and it’s warranted given what we saw from them 
last season. Still, if either one ends up hoisting the trophy, it’ll mark 
the first time since 2014 that the preseason favorite has won.
Considering all of that, let’s get into some picks to win the Heisman 
Trophy in 2026. Here are four of my favorites, but I’ll also mention 
that I’m closely monitoring Alabama’s quarterback competition 
between Keelon Russell and Austin Mack. 
DARIAN MENSAH
MIAMI (12-1) 
Nobody’s raiding the portal quite like Mario Cristobal. With 
the help of offensive guru Shannon Dawson, Miami has landed 
Cam Ward, Carson Beck, and now Mensah in the portal era. The 
Hurricanes helped Ward become the No. 1 pick in the 2025 NFL 
Draft, as he was undeniable after throwing for 4,313 yards with 39 
touchdowns and only seven picks in his final college season. Beck 
didn’t go in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft, but he was picked 
in the third after throwing for 3,813 yards and 30 touchdowns. Now 
it’s Mensah’s turn to go to work in this quarterback-friendly system.
Mensah arguably arrives in Coral Gables as a more polished player 
than Ward and Beck were at the same stage. Last season, despite 
being surrounded by underwhelming talent, Mensah threw for 3,973 
yards with 34 touchdowns and only six interceptions. He also posted a 
PFF passer grade of 85.0. Mensah is extremely dangerous throwing to 
every part of the field, makes big-time throws in the face of pressure, 
and has played in some massive games. He’s the total package.
Mensah now gets to play for one of the biggest brands in football, and 
he’ll be surrounded by weapons. Malachi Toney was one of the best 
players in college football last season, Cooper Barkate was Mensah’s 
top receiver at Duke, and Miami has high hopes for 6-foot-4 sophomore 
Joshua Moore. Mensah will also be working behind a better offensive 
line than he had in either of his previous two college seasons.
There’s a real chance Mensah puts up ridiculous numbers for a 
Hurricanes team that should win double-digit games and reach the 
College Football Playoff. That makes him the best of the chalkier 
options when you’re looking at the Heisman Trophy odds.
JOHN MATEER
OKLAHOMA (25-1)
It’s a little surprising to see Mateer available at 25-1 odds. Early 
last season, Mateer looked like he was on his way to winning the 
Heisman Trophy. Through four games, he was putting up absurd 
numbers as both a thrower and a runner. But a broken thumb on 
his throwing hand changed everything. Mateer came back and 
threw three interceptions against Texas on October 11, and it felt 
like he was never the same quarterback afterward.
Mateer enters the 2026 season at full strength. That means he should 
hit the ground running, even with Oklahoma playing a difficult 
schedule. Mateer is back in Ben Arbuckle’s offense, which he’s 
mastered at this point. He also has an excellent group of pass-catching 
options and should be operating behind an improved offensive line.
Rushing upside has always mattered when it comes to this award, 
and that gives Mateer something other candidates don’t have. Two 
years ago, Mateer rushed for 826 yards and 15 touchdowns for 
Washington State. He might not have that in him in the SEC, but his 
legs will still be a major factor for the Sooners.
With so many showcase games on the schedule — at Michigan, at 
Georgia, vs. Texas, vs. Ole Miss, vs. Texas A&M — Mateer has a real 
chance to rack up Heisman moments. Oklahoma just needs the 
slightest bit of team success to put him back in the conversation. 
MARCEL REED
TEXAS A&M (30-1) 
Reed didn’t receive any votes for this award last season, but he wasn’t 
far off from having a seat at the table. Reed threw for 3,169 yards 
with 25 touchdowns, rushed for 493 yards and six scores, and was 
the drink-stirrer for one of the best teams in college football. With 
another year of experience, things are likely to ramp up a little.
Texas A&M will have a new offensive coordinator in Holmon 
Wiggins, but he was the wide receivers coach and co-offensive 
coordinator last season. That means this offense shouldn’t change 
too much, and it’s one Reed is fully comfortable with. The Aggies 
don’t ask too much of him as a passer, but he’s capable of making 
most throws. There’s also room for improvisation, and that’s where 
Reed’s elite rushing ability shows up.
Reed is going to have a very good wide receiver group this season, 
with Mario Craver, a first-team All-SEC performer last year, leading 
the pack. He’s also going to have a large offensive line blocking for 
him. Reed just needs to cut down on his interceptions, as the 12 
he threw in 2025 were unacceptable. Reed also happened to throw 
eight of those in his final five games, meaning he made his biggest 
mistakes in the biggest games.
With one more year of seasoning, and improved decision-making, 
Reed should make a real run at the Heisman. At the very least, 
a healthy Reed should make a strong early case, presenting 
opportunities to monetize a ticket later on. If Texas A&M can pick up a 
road win over LSU on September 26, there’s a good chance the Aggies 
will be 7-0 heading into a road game against Alabama on October 24.
DREW MESTEMAKER
OKLAHOMA STATE (75-1) 
Mestemaker led all of FBS in passing yards last year, throwing for 
4,379 yards, 34 touchdowns, and nine interceptions in a masterful 
freshman season. He then decided to follow head coach Eric 
Morris from North Texas to Oklahoma State, where he’ll be playing 
alongside several of his former teammates.
Mestemaker will have to adjust to a significant jump in 
competition, facing strong Big 12 defenses after seeing nothing but 
soft AAC units. Still, Mestemaker should be able to handle it. He’s a 
future first-round pick playing behind a better offensive line, he has 
serious talent at the skill positions, and he knows this offense like 
the back of his hand.
It’s just hard to imagine this being anything but a massive season for 
Mestemaker, but grabbing him means hoping for some team success 
at Oklahoma State. That’s the main concern here. The Cowboys are 
going to be excellent offensively, but will the defense be able to get 
off the field? The lineup on the defensive side of the ball features only 
four players with starting experience, so new defensive coordinator 
Skyler Cassity will be banking on a bunch of unknown commodities.
Making the College Football Playoff isn’t a requirement for Heisman 
contention, but Mestemaker probably needs to win eight or so 
games to really win voters over. That might be unlikely in Year 1, 
but he’s worth a flier at 75-1.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
Last year was an eye-opener for my “world-famous” college football 
stability system. Prior to the 2025 campaign, I shared my concern about 
how program stability was changing, largely because of the transfer 
portal. However, since the system had only suffered a single losing 
season since 2013, I figured I owed it to VSiN readers to go with the 
methodology “as-is.” Well, unfortunately, that backfired a bit for me 
and for everyone who has benefited from the Stability System for many 
years, as the final record wound up being just 30-36 ATS. I promised that 
I would dig into the nuts and bolts of the concept to see whether what 
I was doing still made sense in this new era. I did and now have some 
new data to share. 
The College Football Stability System is for the first four weeks of every 
season (Weeks 0, 1, 2, and 3). It is the foremost strategy I employ every 
year to find value early. The thought behind it is that teams in more 
stable year-to-year situations are better bets early, while those that have 
undergone significant offseason change should be faded. I feel the 
logic is fundamentally sound. Returning fewer starters, starting over 
at quarterback, and welcoming new head coaches or coordinators are 
always hurdles for teams.
One of the biggest areas of transition for teams nowadays is the transfer 
of starting quarterbacks. To me, the position is of such importance that 
a transfer quarterback for a team, even if he has three years of starting 
experience somewhere else, I still consider him a NEW quarterback, or 
more effectively, a change at QB. He is still learning new schemes, and 
while his veteran experience may lessen some of the bumps along the 
way, there are still hurdles to overcome early on with this new player 
in this most key position. There can be degrees to this; however, in the 
current era, some QBs, such as Rocco Becht of Penn State, followed 
their former school’s head coach and OC to a new school. To me, this 
is still a big change. So, to clarify how I am dealing with the transfer 
portal starters, here is your answer: I consider former starters acquired 
through the transfer portal at non-QB positions as starters.
This is where the new numbers and changes will come in. I have 
conducted regression analysis on my College Football Stability System 
and here are the results. First off, my results still did show that the 
FIRST FOUR WEEKS (0, 1, 2, and 3) were the most impacted by stability. 
So, I will be sticking with that. Also, since most of the changes I’ve seen 
in the college football world have occurred since the COVID season, I 
have looked back at the results of the various stability factors in the first 
four weeks after 2021. Here are those results. Note that these trends only 
include FBS vs. FBS games.
•	
NEW head coaches are 91-153 SU and 110-132 ATS (45.4%) in the 
first four weeks of the CFB season versus returning head coaches 
since 2021 
•	
NEW offensive coordinators are 157-203 SU and 177-178 ATS 
(49.9%) in the first four weeks of the CFB season versus returning 
offensive coordinators since 2021 
•	
NEW defensive coordinators are 165-198 SU and 163-195 ATS 
(45.5%) in the first four weeks of the CFB season versus returning 
defensive coordinators since 2021 
•	
NEW starting quarterbacks are 159-178 SU and 157-172 ATS (47.7%) 
in the first four weeks of the CFB season versus returning defensive 
coordinators since 2021 
•	
Teams with 0-7 total returning starters are 21-60 SU and 40-41 ATS 
(49.4%) in the first four weeks of the CFB season versus teams 
returning 8+ since 2021 
•	
Teams with 17+ total returning starters are 107-89 SU and 108-86 
ATS (55.7%) in the first four weeks of the CFB season versus teams 
returning 16 or fewer since 2021
From this info, bettors can certainly discern that having new head 
coaches, new defensive coordinators, and many returning starters are 
the most impactful offseason developments.
I also recognized that CONFERENCE GAMES on my stability system 
were pulling down the winning percentages. In fact, teams with an old 
stability edge of seven points or more in conference games were only 
winning around 49.5% ATS. 
The other two things I found that were negatively impacting my Stability 
System results were 1) games with point spreads of 30+ and 2) leaving 
out teams with an edge of 6 on the stability scores.
With the stats above in mind, my official new College Football Stability 
System(s) will read as follows:
Play ON any team with a STABILITY SCORE EDGE of 6+ in non-conference 
games in the first four weeks of the season (weeks 0, 1, 2, 3), assuming the 
game DOES NOT have a point spread of -30 or higher for either team. (335-
222 SU and 302-243-12 ATS, 55.4% since 2013)
AND 
Play AGAINST any team with STABILITY SCORES of 0-6 in non-conference 
games in the first four weeks of the season (weeks 0, 1, 2, 3) versus teams 
with higher scores, assuming the game DOES NOT have a point spread of 
-30 or higher for either team (FADE record 259-136 SU and 217-173-4 ATS, 
55.6% since 2013)
Doing regression on the tweaked Stability Score Edge System, I found 
that over the last 13 years, there were only two losing seasons, one of 
them being last year. The second angle, teams with 0-6 scores, even lost 
a year ago, as they were 22-26 ATS. In my opinion, both systems are still 
very viable.
Just below, I’ve put together a chart of the College Football Stability 
Scores for 2026. When the season arrives, I will put together lists in each 
of the first four weeks detailing the top mismatches. Again, I have now 
found that a Stability Mismatch score of 6 is the minimum on which I 
will consider a play for this thought process in non-conference games. 
Incidentally, USC (15) hosting San Jose State (7) in Week 0 would be a 
play for 2026 except the Trojans are 35.5-point favorites. Instead, Hawaii 
(14) -3.5 at Stanford (3) and UNLV (10) -3.5 hosting Memphis (2) are the 
first two playable games for Week 0.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
A year ago, Fernando Mendoza did not top 
any preseason lists that ranked the elite 
quarterbacks in college football, and that 
turned out to be a big miss by many analysts. 
Mendoza managed to outplay several other 
overhyped quarterbacks en route to winning 
the Heisman Trophy, leading Indiana to the 
national championship and becoming the No. 
1 pick in the NFL Draft.
The importance of the quarterback to a team’s 
success is obvious, but scouting the position 
accurately is not 
always easy.
In 2024, a record 
six quarterbacks 
were selected 
in the first 
round of the 
draft, including 
the first three 
overall picks. 
Now, after back-
to-back down 
years at the 
position, some 
analysts believe 
the 2027 draft 
could challenge 
the first-round 
record.
Time will tell, but this has the potential to 
be “The Year of the Quarterback” in college 
football. While names like Manning, Chambliss 
and Carr are certain to garner their share of 
headlines during the upcoming season, the 
depth of this year’s class is what sets it apart.
Without further ado, this is how I rank the top 
quarterbacks entering this season.
2. TRINIDAD CHAMBLISS, OLE MISS
Was there a better single-game performance 
in 2025 than the masterpiece turned in by 
Chambliss in the Rebels’ 39-34 CFP quarterfinal 
win over Georgia? Eluding would-be Dawg 
defenders play after play, the Ferris State transfer 
threw for 362 yards against one of the nation’s 
stingiest stop units. Currently listed at 15-1 to win 
the Heisman, one could argue Chambliss is the 
best betting option on the board.
3. CJ CARR, NOTRE DAME
Manning and Chambliss share top billing, but it 
would be no surprise if Carr hoisted the hardware 
in Manhattan come the second Saturday in 
December. Draft analyst Todd McShay hailed 
Carr as the MVP at the recent Manning Passing 
Academy, proclaiming “it wasn’t even close.” 
The Irish are legitimate national championship 
contenders, so Carr’s possibilities for individual 
and team accolades seem endless.
4. DANTE MOORE, OREGON
After struggling as a true freshman at UCLA and 
then sitting behind Dillon Gabriel at Oregon as 
a sophomore, the Detroit native showed why 
he was one of the top recruits in the Class of 
2023, leading the Ducks to the CFP semifinals 
last season. Moore was projected by some as a 
potential top-five selection in this past April’s 
draft, but he opted to return to school.
5. GUNNER STOCKTON, GEORGIA
Despite an NIL deal reportedly north of $1 
million, Stockton drives a hand-me-down 1984 
Ford F-150 pickup gifted by his grandfather 
with over 300,000 miles. Like his truck, he’s 
an old-school throwback who may not throw 
the prettiest ball yet competes with grit and 
comes through in clutch moments.
6. JULIAN SAYIN, OHIO STATE
With college football’s top pass catcher, 
Jeremiah Smith, and an embarrassment of 
other riches at his disposal, Sayin is a solid 
bet to post Heisman-worthy numbers in his 
second season as the Buckeyes’ starter. Games 
against Texas, Indiana, USC, Oregon and 
Michigan certainly provide the platform to 
attract the voters’ attention. At a double-digit 
price (12-1 at Circa), Sayin may be worth a 
look in the Heisman market.
7. JOHN MATEER, OKLAHOMA
Opinions are mixed on Mateer, who was 
hindered by a bum thumb on his throwing 
hand throughout much of the 2025 campaign. 
Supporters say he’s among the nation’s elite at his 
position, while detractors want more evidence 
against top-shelf opposition. The tough Texan is a 
true dual threat, having rushed for 847 yards and 
15 TDs in 2024 at Washington State.
8. LANORRIS SELLERS, SOUTH CAROLINA
Gamecock quarterbacks have been sacked 
more than 40 times in each of the past three 
seasons. With more experience up front, the 
dynamic Sellers could shine with additional 
time to operate. At 6-3 and 245 pounders, 
Sellers is a load to bring down as evidenced 
by his 674 rushing yards in 2024. For those 
dreaming of a bigger Heisman payout, Sellers 
is currently 50-1 at the Westgate SuperBook.
9. SAM LEAVITT, LSU
After guiding Arizona State to the first-ever 
12-team CFP in 2024, Leavitt’s production 
dipped last season, primarily because of a 
foot injury which shortened his season by five 
games. The dual-threat Leavitt might not have 
a Cam Skattebo in his arsenal, but the Tigers’ 
receivers may be among the nation’s finest 
after scoring big in the portal.
10. DARIAN MENSAH, MIAMI
Coming out of St. Joseph High School in Santa 
Maria, Calif., Mensah was a largely-ignored 
two-star prospect who ultimately ended up with 
just two offers: Tulane and Idaho State. After 
spending one season each at Tulane and Duke, 
Mensah (56 career passing TDs) steps into the 
South Beach spotlight as he attempts to guide 
the Hurricanes back to the playoff.
11. BEAR 
BACHMEIER, 
BYU
As a true 
freshman, 
Bachmeier 
threw for 3,000 
yards or more, 
rushed for 
500 or more, 
accounted for 
at least 25 TDs, 
and had 10 or 
fewer turnovers, 
becoming only 
the 19th power 
conference 
quarterback to 
accomplish that 
feat in the past 20 
years. With a full offseason to sharpen his skills, 
Bachmeier is an intriguing Heisman long shot at 
80/1 at Westgate.
12. MARCEL REED, TEXAS A&M
At his best, Reed can beat opponents with his 
arm (more than 5,000 yards passing across 
the past two seasons) and legs (more than 
1,000 yards rushing during the same term). At 
his worst, the Nashville product has turned 
the ball over 21 times in 21 career starts - 
including a total of five in back-to-back losses 
to Texas and Miami to end the 2025 season.
13. JAYDEN MAIAVA, USC
The Honolulu native began his career at 
UNLV, but a stellar freshman season there in 
2023 (almost 3,100 yards passing) caught the 
eye of Lincoln Riley and others. Maiava has a 
big arm, but needs to protect the football (26 
interceptions in three seasons) and perform 
better on the road. If he does those things 
and new receivers emerge, he could be a dark 
horse contender for national honors.
14. BYRUM BROWN, AUBURN
The 6-foot-3, 232-pound dual-threat Brown had 
better rushing (1,008 yards) and passing (3,158 
yards) numbers at South Florida last season 
than Mateer did at Washington State in 2024. If 
Brown remains healthy, the Tigers could throw 
a wrench in someone’s playoff plans.
15. CJ BAILEY, NORTH CAROLINA STATE
At 6-foot-6 with a quick release and big arm, 
Bailey has certainly attracted the attention of 
NFL scouts. With 22 starts under his belt in 
just two years on campus - if he can refine his 
mechanics and sharpen his accuracy - it’s not 
out of the question that he could ultimately 
play his way into the first round of the draft.
THE YEAR of the quarterback
by Paul Stone
1. ARCH MANNING, TEXAS
Perhaps the most polarizing figure in all of college sports, 
Manning began the 2025 season as the Heisman favorite, but 
he sputtered in September and quickly fell from grace. From 
October on, however, the nephew of two former Super Bowl 
MVPs showcased his talents, throwing for 2,012 yards in the 
season’s final eight games, while accounting for 21 touchdowns 
against just three turnovers during that span. Expect to see the 
Longhorns utilize Manning more in the running game after his 
155-yard rushing outburst against Michigan in the Citrus Bowl.
“
“

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
Putting together my college football power ratings for the 2026 
season involves analyzing the returning players/coaches for 
the teams, making adjustments based on last year’s finish and 
the current perception of teams, and also ensuring I have not 
assumed anything out of the window for normalcy for each 
team’s recent history or conference strength. That last point has 
become a bigger challenge each passing year as some teams 
completely revamp their rosters through the transfer portal.
Only 52 teams are returning their starting quarterbacks from 
last season, and several of the country’s most prominent teams 
from a year ago are not, most notably title game participants 
Indiana and Miami (FL). If you’re thinking the coaching 
carousel was significant in the offseason, the 33 changes to 
programs this season in that regard are a fairly high number.
Last year, of the five teams from the Power Four (or 
Independent) that I projected to win 10+ games in this same 
exercise, only one of them made the CFP. However, the year 
before, four of the five made up the four semifinal teams. For 
2026, there are seven teams that are projected to win 10+ games, 
and that group is Notre Dame (11.2), Texas Tech (10.7), Oregon 
(10.3), Indiana (10.2), Miami (FL) (10.1), Ohio State (10.0) and 
Georgia (10.0). As you look at the conference overview pages, 
you’ll see other teams such as Penn State, Texas, and BYU that 
could join those frontrunners.
I’ve taken my adjusted power numbers for 2026 and run them 
against the complete schedule to project the season standings. 
You will also find a listing of all 138 FBS teams and their 
schedules, with my projected power ratings lines for each game.
Before unleashing the projections, however, let’s look at some of 
the highlights from the analysis:
•	
According to my figures, after two straight seasons 
of Florida playing the toughest schedule nationally, 
Texas takes over for 2026, at least as it stands now. The 
Longhorns are ranked just ahead of Oklahoma, Kentucky, 
Mississippi State, and Arkansas in that regard, all SEC 
teams. My projections have the Longhorns finishing at 
9-3 in the regular season, but I could easily be talked into 
more, as I believe they are a legit national title contender. 
The schedules of the other four SEC teams on the list are 
mostly due to conference opponents. The first non-SEC 
team on the list is Michigan at No. 6. 
•	
The “easiest” schedule this season belongs to UMass, 
who unseats Liberty for that honor after the Flames 
held the designation for the last three seasons. The 
Minutemen’s 2026 opponents average a 26.21 power 
rating. To put that in perspective, it would be like playing 
a team at Bowling Green’s level every week for an entire 
season. Even still, my numbers call for them to go just 
3.4-8.6 this season. However, even with an easier slate 
last season, UMass went 0-12. In terms of other weak 
schedules, Buffalo, Sacramento State, and Ohio, all other 
MAC teams as well, check in at Nos. 2-4. The first non-
MAC team on the weak schedule list is Jacksonville State, 
at No. 5, out of Conference USA. For the record, Liberty 
is the No. 6. 
•	
Notre Dame has the highest win projection of any team, 
with 11.2, a half win better than Texas Tech (10.7). Oregon 
(10.3), Indiana (10.2), and Miami (FL) (10.1) round out the 
top five. The only other double-digit win projections go to 
Ohio State and Georgia. 
•	
Assuming the projections play out accurately, besides 
Texas Tech, Oregon, Indiana, Miami (FL), and Ohio State 
the other Power Four conference teams that would be 
expected to contend for a spot in the College Football 
Playoff this year would be Georgia, Texas, Penn State, BYU, 
and perhaps SMU or Utah. All of those teams are expected 
to win 8.9 or more regular-season games, according to my 
projections. Some of the intriguing “longshot” contenders 
could include Alabama, Texas A&M, LSU, and USC. 
•	
Boise State (9.2), James Madison (9.1), UNLV (9.0), and 
Navy (8.5), and New Mexico (8.5) have the highest 
projected win totals among the Group of Six teams, 
although each faces an early test or two that might prevent 
them from going undefeated and challenging for the 
coveted CFP spot. 
•	
In terms of teams expected to improve from last season, 
either by an enhanced power rating or projected wins 
compared to last regular season, Oklahoma State (+14) and 
Virginia Tech (+10) are the two teams I have with double-
digit power rating increases. In terms of the biggest win 
total gains expected for this season, the projections call for 
OSU (+4.7), VT (+4.3), and Liberty (+4.1) to all win at least 
four games more than a season ago. 
•	
There are a crazy number of eight teams that drop by 10 
points or more in my power ratings for the 2026 preseason 
when compared to last year’s finish. The biggest loser, 
if you will, is North Texas, who falls by a huge 14-point 
downgrade. It’s not hard to understand why when you 
realize that new head coach Neal Brown is taking over 
virtually a brand-new team, one with no starter back from 
the 2025 group that went 12-2 and scored 45.1 PPG. 
•	
Other big drops belong with James Madison (-12.5) and 
Tulane (-11.5), two other complete rebuilds for new 
coaches. The worst drops among P4 programs belong to 
Vanderbilt (-10.5) and Iowa State (-10). 
•	
In terms of biggest win total declines compared to the 2025 
regular season, you’ll find North Texas (-5.1), North Dakota 
State (-4.0), Connecticut (-3.7), and Vanderbilt (-3.6) at the 
top of the list. Perhaps the most interesting team among 
that group is NDSU, who moves up to FBS for the first 
time and figures to see better and more consistent tough 
competition on a weekly basis in the Mountain West. 
•	
In terms of the projections and how they correlate to the 
Season Win Totals offered up at DraftKings, here are the 
biggest differences. Teams expected to win more games 
than their DK win props include Boise State (+1.7), UNLV 
(+1.5), Arkansas State (+1.3), Miami (OH) (+1.3), Georgia 
Southern (+1.3), Western Kentucky (+1.2), and Navy (+1.0) 
as the teams exceeding a 1.0 difference. The Broncos +1.7 
difference represents one of the biggest I’ve ever had in 
this exercise, and I even double- and triple-checked the 
numbers to be sure. I think the oddsmakers are giving a bit 
too much credit to the strength of the new Pac-12, and in 
my opinion, BSU is the obvious favorite. I guess the same 
goes for the Runnin’ Rebels, who figure to benefit greatly 
from Boise leaving the Mountain West. 
•	
Teams expected to fall short of their season win props 
by the biggest margins include Northern Illinois (-1.1), 
Georgia State (-1.0), Florida (-0.9), Sam Houston State (-0.8), 
and Cal (-0.8). Interestingly, Northern Illinois makes a 
jump in conference strength by moving from the MAC to 
the Mountain West. Also, Florida gets a new head coach 
in Jon Sumrall, who seems to have the enthusiasm meter 
pegged, but perhaps not the roster yet to compete in what 
looks like a very strong and balanced SEC. In general, I’m 
not a fan of big conference teams making regular coaching 
changes when it appears some progress is being made, as 
it sets the program back usually.
Throughout this year’s Guide, you will find my projected 
standings for each of the conferences. The teams are sorted by 
CONFERENCE WINS. You will also find their season win total 
from DraftKings, their 2026 Steve Makinen Power Rating, Home 
and Road Field Ratings, Schedule Strength & National Ranking, 
plus their overall & conference record projections.

2026 VSiN COLLEGE FOOTBALL BETTING GUIDE
The American Conference seems pretty wide-open for the 2026 season and it’s fair to wonder if any team will have the 
record or resume to represent the Group of Six in the College Football Playoff. There are four new head coaches and five 
second-year head coaches in the conference, so nine of the league’s 14 teams are tough to project. Tenured coaches might 
have an inside track this season, but anything could happen.
In terms of preseason conference winner odds, only the MAC has a higher-priced favorite than the American and seven 
of the 14 teams are priced at +800 or lower. Navy is the tepid favorite here with one of the more tenured coaches in the 
conference, as Brian Newberry begins his fourth season at the helm. UTSA’s Jeff Traylor and Army’s Jeff Monken are 
the only two sideline bosses with more years under their belts than Newberry. It probably isn’t a coincidence that UTSA 
(+480) and Army (6-1) are the second and third favorites, respectively, behind Navy (+310).
Life is tough in the American Conference for college football these days. As mentioned, nine of the 14 teams have head 
coaches hired within the last two seasons because this conference is a springboard to Power Four jobs. Furthermore, 
any players that stand out are going to be on the minds of SEC, ACC, Big Ten, and Big 12 teams that are looking to fill 
some voids and plug some holes. In some respects, the service academies have an advantage in that they aren’t watching 
players go out the door for NIL paydays, but they also can’t leverage the transfer portal to their advantage.
Outside of Army and Navy, just about every program in the conference has fewer than 10 returning starters. But, that 
doesn’t mean they are immune to big personnel losses, especially in Navy’s case with QB Blake Horvath.
In a high-variance conference, there should be money to be made, whether you can isolate overachievers or 
underachievers with props and futures before the season or on a weekly basis.

Can Cale complete the season?
That’s Cale Hellums, Army’s starting QB, who split time last season 
to a degree with Dewayne Coleman. The 5-foot-10 Hellums had 
304 carries last season for 1,223 yards and 18 TDs. He added 
four passing TDs and 694 yards as well. But, that’s a really brutal 
workload for a smaller-statured guy and something that obviously 
has to be considered with any long-term position on Army. 
It’s entirely possible that Monken and OC Cody Worley found 
something in converted QB and all-name-team member Godspower 
Nwawuihe, who ran for 171 yards in the Fenway Bowl. Considering 
Noah Short, Hayden Reed, Coleman, and Briggs Bartosh are all 
gone, somebody has to help Hellums with rush attempts, as he had 
nearly 41% of the carries.
Will the conference adjust to Army in Year 3?
This will be Army’s third year in the American. So far, they are 12-4 
in league play, but that mark is a tale of two seasons with an 8-0 
record in Year 1 and a 4-4 record in Year 2. When Navy joined the 
AAC in 2015, they went 7-1 in league play in each of their first two 
seasons before dropping to 4-4 in Year 3 and then 2-6 in Year 4. The 
absences of Daily and Udoh absolutely played a role, but the Black 
Knights had 5.7 YPC in 2024 and 4.38 YPC in 2025 in conference 
games. Army is also +12 in TO margin in two years of conference 
play. Obviously their style of play limits the potential for turnovers, 
but it’s still something to think about.
Who is going to step up on defense?
DC Nate Woody is now in Cincinnati, so pass game coordinator 
Daryl Dixon, not to be confused with The Walking Dead character 
of the same name, has that role. Dixon has been with the program 
for the last 10 seasons, so he’s very familiar with the scheme and 
the types of players that Army has on defense. It’s almost always an 
undersized unit in the trenches, but often an experienced crew. This 
season is a bit of an exception. While there are a lot of seniors on 
the two-deep, the top seven tacklers are all gone, including Andon 
Thomas, who led the team with 113 tackles. Dixon, who has mostly 
coached defensive backs, needs to find more negative plays, as the 
Black Knights only had 15 sacks.

At least there’s nowhere to go but up, right?!
The bar has been set so low at Charlotte now that I’m not even 
sure a toddler could crawl under it. Since joining the FBS ranks 
over a decade ago, Charlotte has one bowl game appearance. Last 
season was probably as close to rock bottom as it has gotten. The 
defense managed just 14 sacks, the offense had just 2.7 yards per 
carry, and a lot of it had to do with how painfully thin the roster was 
when Albin took the job. Neither the incoming class nor the portal 
class graded all that highly for 247Sports relative to the rest of the 
conference, but there are a lot more warm bodies and some of them 
are probably better at football than the ones that were there.
Is there a starting QB on the roster?
Charlotte’s boosters and supporters did open their wallets to try and 
get Albin a real QB last season, picking up Grayson Loftis from Duke 
and Conner Harrell from North Carolina. Harrell suffered a season-
ending injury after emerging as the better option with a 66.7% 
completion rate and a 4/2 TD/INT ratio, leaving it in the hands of 
Loftis, who had an 8/8 TD/INT ratio with just a 55% completion 
rate. Even Zach Wilcke got some reps, though he’s since moved on. 
This season, the starting gig may fall on the shoulders of Western 
Carolina transfer Cole Gonzales, at least until Harrell returns. None 
of the options are particularly good. On the plus side, almost all the 
backs and receivers are new, which can only help after last season’s 
4.6 YPP.
Where’s the beef?
One of the problems that plagued Charlotte last season, and has 
clearly been a thing for several years now, is that they are not big 
enough or strong enough up front. Last year’s team was -2.3 in yards 
per carry differential. The team before that was -1.6 YPC. The 2019 
Charlotte team had a positive YPC differential and that’s the one 
that went bowling. Not to mention, the 49ers haven’t had more than 
20 sacks in a season since that ‘19 campaign. Prior to becoming the 
OC at Ohio, Albin primarily coached offensive linemen and running 
backs. Clearly the athletic department felt the same way when 
they hired Biff Poggi in terms of the team’s lack of toughness in the 
trenches. If Albin can improve that, he can find some momentum.

More run or more shoot?
The new OC is Jordan Davis and that means a scheme change in 
Greenville. Davis was working under Eric Morris at North Texas, an 
offense that led the nation in points per game with over 45, yards 
per game with just over 512, and ranked third in yards per play. 
While the prevailing thought would be that a Morris-led offense 
would just chuck the ball around the field, that wasn’t the case. 
Drew Mestemaker threw for nearly 4,400 yards and had 463 pass 
attempts, but RB Caleb Hawkins had 231 carries for 1,434 yards 
and the team had 517 rush attempts. Davis got backup RB Ashton 
Gray to transfer and also WR Landon Sides, so he has skill guys who 
know the scheme. The ECU run game actually fell from 4.8 yards 
per carry to 4.1, so that has a good chance to go back up.
Who will run the show?
Well, that’s the biggest question for ECU from a personnel 
standpoint. Miami transfer Emory Williams and now four-time 
transfer Mitch Griffis, who was at Texas Tech last season, are the 
main options. Williams is the bigger, more athletic option, but 
Griffis may more closely resemble Mestemaker’s skill set, though he 
doesn’t have the size. Katin Houser, another portal find by Harrell, 
who really seems to have his finger on the pulse of free agency, 
was very solid last season. Whether it’s Williams or Griffis, good 
numbers should come again. The offensive line could be shaky at 
the outset, which perhaps puts Williams in the driver’s seat for the 
job.
Can Harrell work his magic again?
With two returning starters back on defense, Harrell and DC Josh 
Aldridge did a masterful job. The Pirates allowed just 20.1 PPG and 
just over 5.1 YPP. Statistically, everything got better. The team was 
better against the run, generated more sacks, and the defense had 
24 takeaways leading to a +10 TO margin. It does need to be said 
that the Pirates allowed just 390 yards in their wins over Campbell 
and Coastal Carolina and 71 rushing yards on 53 carries, so their 
conference numbers weren’t nearly as strong as the full body of 
work suggests. That said, ECU still outgained American foes by 
0.65 YPP, as the offense got stronger as the season went along. He’s 
basically starting from scratch in terms of returning starters and 
has a new DC this time around.

The makings of a good football 
team were present in Boca Raton 
last season. Even though Florida 
Atlantic finished 4-8, failing to 
reach six wins for the sixth straight 
season, you could see Zach Kittley’s 
plan in motion. The youngest 
coach in FBS, and big proponent 
of the Air Raid offense, had plenty 
of growing pains. One stat stood 
out well above the rest - the Owls 
were -21 in TO margin. Clean that 
up and we might have something 
here. It will be up to Caden

This will be a high-variance team

the guys that fit and don’t fit what 
he’s aiming to achieve. Last season

and he did double duty as the

projection is 5.64 wins.

Are we in the Caden Veltkamp camp?
Veltkamp is really the only starting QB for FAU and he needs to 
be better. Drew Devillier transferred in from Rice and redshirt 
freshman Jordan Magwood threw nine passes last season. 
Veltkamp was asked to throw a lot and FAU did trail a lot, so the 
17 interceptions may not all be on him, especially considering he 
had just 11 of them in three seasons at Western Kentucky. Easton 
Messer caught 104 balls for 1,052 yards and several others saw work 
in this scheme, including returnee Dominique Henry. Guys will 
put up numbers, but Messer is still the only true go-to guy and that 
could continue to hold Veltkamp back and the rest of the team by 
extension. Veltkamp threw seven picks over the first three games 
and six over the last three games, so he did show he could take care 
of the ball in the middle of the season. A silver lining, perhaps.
Can Kittley find some balance on offense?
The rushing numbers were downright laughable for the Owls. They 
averaged 105 yards on 3.5 yards per carry and even mustered just 
82 yards and 2.9 yards per carry in American Conference play. This 
is not exactly a conference known for a lot of physical, stalwart 
defenses, but there were no holes on the ground whatsoever. The 
OL was shifting to a very pass-heavy blocking scheme, so maybe 
that had something to do with it. While the OL has a lot of new faces 
and some guys playing new positions, the running back room looks 
more intriguing. Kaden Shields-Dutton had 5.5 yards per carry and 
Kittley went the JUCO route to get Leonard Farrow, who averaged 
over seven yards per carry at Fairmont State. If a running game 
and more ball control are attainable, that will help the defense 
tremendously.
Will the Owls stop the run?
The FAU defensive line was objectively terrible last season. 
American Conference foes ran for an average of 232 yards per 
game and that even includes a 68-yard performance from UAB. 
While the offense needs work, and the offensive line is very light on 
experience, Kittley and his staff really hammered the defensive side 
of the ball in the portal. Some guys are in Year 2 of the scheme and 
others are newcomers to the roster, but you can tell that the DL and 
really the front seven in general were focal points. It is wild to think 
that FAU averaged a 150-yard differential in rushing yards over their 
eight conference games. That simply cannot happen again.

My projection is 7.38 wins.

What will this offense look like?
Huff went back to the Sun Belt for his OC, as Kevin Decker was at 
Old Dominion the last few years. Decker led an ODU offense that 
ranked in the top 20 in yards per play and averaged 32 PPG. He had 
a Fordham offense that averaged over 600 yards per game back in 
2021. This is a guy who believes in a high-octane, explosive offense 
that starts with the ground game and the pass comes off of it. The 
Monarchs averaged 5.6 yards per carry and nearly 240 rushing 
yards per game. How all the transfer pieces and parts fit in will be 
fascinating to see. Marcus Stokes was a multi-year starter at West 
Florida and Air Noland was a very highly-touted recruit who never 
saw the field at Ohio State and transferred to South Carolina.
Who are the impact players on offense?
Whether it’s Stokes, Noland, or maybe even Huff recruit Denzel 
Gardner, there still aren’t any truly experienced or established skill-
position guys. Dallan Hayden had over five yards per carry at Ohio 
State, but was ineffective at Colorado. Jaylin Carter only had 166 
yards last season at Southern Miss and Manny Covey had under 300 
yards in three seasons at Cincinnati. The wide receivers are all in a 
similar boat, as some of them have impressive yards per reception 
numbers, but not many receptions. This is basically a bunch of 
noteworthy recruits who couldn’t crack the lineup at their previous 
schools, so all of them have chips on their shoulders. That could 
make for a fun offense, especially if Decker can play with tempo.
Will the defense suffer as a result of the offense?
Huff made a really, really good DC hire in Lance Guidry, who he 
worked with at Marshall and has been a DC at many different 
places. Like the offense, virtually nobody who played for the Tigers 
last season is on the roster, so this unit has been revamped via 
the portal as well. Huff did bring several Golden Eagles with him, 
including J’Mond Tapp, who had 7.5 sacks, and Ian Foster and 
Anthony Richard, who both had 10 pass breakups. There aren’t as 
many noteworthy recruits on defense, so the upside of the defense 
might be lower than that of the offense, but the collection of 
Southern Miss players should help.

to Navy head coach Brian 
Newberry for bringing in OC

is possible. My projection, 
though, is for 7.56 wins.

How can Navy replicate the wrath of Horvath?
Horvath will be talked about in the same breath as Keenan 
Reynolds and Malcolm Perry. Every few years, it seems like a stud 
QB comes around in Annapolis and Horvath will be held in that 
light. He threw for over 3,000 yards and ran for over 2,600 yards. 
Only Reynolds and Bill Byrne have thrown more passing TDs in 
Navy history. It should also be noted that Reynolds played four 
years, while Horvath played three. Braxton Woodson has some 
enormous shoes to fill. He’s plenty familiar with the scheme, having 
started games the last two seasons and being used when Horvath 
was banged up. In fact, Woodson had 9.4 yards per carry on his 
44 attempts last season. But, Horvath (58.8%) only trailed Roger 
Staubach in completion percentage with at least 120 pass attempts. 
Woodson is not that kind of thrower with a 46.3% completion rate.
What about the other losses?
Tecza and Heidenreich, who was drafted in the seventh round by 
the Steelers, are monumental losses of production as well. Tecza 
ran for 902 yards on 5.7 yards per carry with 10 rushing TD last 
season and ended his Navy career 12th in rushing yards with 2,236. 
Tecza is seventh all-time among running backs in rushing yards. 
Heidenreich had over 500 yards on the ground and 941 yards on 51 
catches. He passed Rob Taylor for the program’s lead in receiving 
yards and finished his career fifth in scrimmage yards. Oh, and 
fourth-leading rusher and second-leading receiver Brandon 
Chatman also exhausted his eligibility. This scheme creates 
productive players, but Navy is missing 93.5% of their passing 
yards, over 83% of their rushing yards, and over 84% of their 
receiving yards from last season.
What does that mean for the defense?
That is the million-dollar question here. Perhaps sensing the 
urgency, Newberry is going back to his roots to serve as his own 
defensive play-caller, even though he demoted P.J. Volker back 
to safeties coach and promoted Eric Lewis to DC. The losses are 
nowhere near as heavy on this side, as five of the top seven tacklers 
are back, but the 5.9 YPP allowed by the Middies last season was 
the most they’ve surrendered since 2021, as were the 25 PPG. Navy’s 
defensive numbers need to be put in the proper context because of 
their offensive scheme, which limits possessions. With a decline in 
offensive production expected, the defense could feel the brunt.

The motto for North Texas football 
this season might be, “Don’t cry 
because it’s over; smile because it 
happened”. Eric Morris is now at 
Oklahoma State after leading the 
Mean Green to probably the best 
season in program history. UNT 
went 12-2, scoring over 45 PPG, 
and won a bowl game for the first 
time since 2013. It will be up to 
Neal Brown to keep the program 
on the map, as Morris and pretty 
much every player of consequence 
has left Denton. Things like this are 
possible in the transfer portal era, 
but this may very well be the most 
stripped-down program we’ve ever 
seen.
The top returning running back 
had 95 yards on 21 carries. The 
top returning pass-catcher had 
seven grabs for 80 yards. The top 
returning tackler had 32 stops 
and 1.5 sacks. The top returning 
DB had four pass breakups. Even 
the kicker and the punter are 
gone. With new schemes and 
new coordinators, having some 
leftover players may not have 
really made that big of a difference 
anyway, but this team is guys who 
played sparingly last season and a 
collection of transfers from every 
corner of the country.
Under 5.5
UNT opens at Indiana and then 
hosts UNLV before visiting Texas 
State to open the season. They’ll 
go to Navy, UTSA, and Tulane, so 
the road games are very difficult. 
The home games are all attainable, 
but UNT might lose every road 
game, leaving no margin for error 
at home. While Jackson is stepping 
down in class with his first non-
Power Four team, he hasn’t taken 
great care of the football. To call it 
a rebuilding year in Denton is an 
understatement. My projection is 
5.81 wins, but I still like the Under.

Who are these f*#%ing guys?
Being a Clevelander, of course one of my favorite movies is Major 
League and the clip of the construction worker looking at the roster 
in the newspaper and asking, “Who are these effing guys?!” after 
the conniving owner cleared out the roster is among the most 
quotable lines. I will say, while all of these guys are new to Denton, 
there are a few notable names. Tayven Jackson originally went to 
Tennessee and got some starts for Indiana and also UCF, so he’s the 
clubhouse leader to be the QB. Jahiem White had 6.5 yards per carry 
at West Virginia, as he rejoined Brown in the Lone Star State. Aaron 
Alexander racked up 91 tackles last season at Arkansas State. But, 
other than those few guys, most of these guys simply didn’t latch on 
at their previous schools.
Is this a better fit for Neal Brown?
Brown is going to be his own OC, which may work out great or may 
not work out at all. It was his work as an OC at Troy, Texas Tech, and 
Kentucky that got him his first head coaching job. Troy didn’t play 
with a ton of tempo or light up the scoreboard while he was there, 
but did score 30+ PPG in each of his last three seasons. West Virginia 
only averaged 30+ PPG in two of his six seasons. Not only are 
expectations exceedingly low with how bare the cupboard is, but 
the North Texas athletic department was willing to go high-octane, 
up-tempo, run-and-shoot style with Morris and his assistants. He 
might be able to reinvent himself, or at least go back to his Texas 
Tech days.
What is the state of the North Texas program?
Sometimes things from above can trickle down to the team 
and create a difficult situation. Even last season, there wasn’t a 
ton of investment in the program. UNT got very fortunate that 
Mestemaker, who had barely played QB in high school, was a stud. 
RB Caleb Hawkins had one Division I offer and it was North Texas. 
He had 25 rushing TDs and over 1,400 yards. Skyler Cassity was 
a stellar DC hire by Morris, but who would have thought it would 
lead to the best defense the program has seen in forever? Will the 
students show up to support a team that has been stripped to the 
studs? Will the athletic department invest more in the roster?

one for Rice, as Scott Abell

Can the offense improve in a hurry under Jacurri?
The Jacurri in question is Jacurri Brown, who spent two years at 
Miami and two years at UCF, but he’s only thrown 148 passes with 
more interceptions (9) than touchdowns (6). What Brown has done, 
though, is effectively run the football. He has 137 carries for 821 
yards, so better than six yards per carry. At Davidson back in 2024, 
Wildcats QBs only had 152 pass attempts in 11 games, as the team 
ran the ball 640 times for 3,720 yards, with QB Andrew Frazier third 
in rush attempts and rush yards. Quinton Jackson was the best 
player on offense for Rice last season with 889 yards and 4.9 yards 
per carry. Last season, the Owls had 647 rush attempts against 224 
pass attempts. I would expect an even starker split this season.
Can the option offense even be successful?
Not all options are created equal, as Navy has recently modified 
theirs and Army just runs theirs like a well-oiled machine, but Rice 
is attempting to do their version of an option in a conference that 
already has two service academies. It makes scheming a lot easier 
for the opposing defense to see a lot of similar core concepts and 
blocking schemes. Rice didn’t face Army last season, but will this 
season. However, they did face Navy and only had 3.1 yards per 
carry. Memphis held them to 2.4 YPC, while UTSA allowed 3.8, UAB 
allowed 3.4, and USF allowed 3.8. Brown could be a difference-
maker as a better runner than Chase Jenkins, but Rice just might 
not be in the best conference for this.
Is everything ‘Kay on defense?
‘Kay as in “okay” under DC Jon Kay, who was a holdover from the 
previous regime. It is a bit surprising that a head coach would 
simply promote the previous head coach’s linebackers coach to 
DC and it didn’t really seem to work out well last season. The Owls 
allowed 6.3 YPP and nearly 33 PPG. It was the worst defensive effort 
for the team since 2022. And, even with a run-heavy approach, the 
team still finished -4 in turnover margin with just seven takeaways. 
Rice was tied for ninth in the nation in turnovers lost and still 
finished with a negative TO margin. The top seven tacklers from last 
season are gone, but starting from scratch probably isn’t a bad thing 
with this defense.

Hype or hope?
Not all highly-touted recruits make it. The transfer portal gives 
players with that kind of pedigree the chance to go to a G6 program 
and attempt to get back on the radar. At USF, most of those players 
are quarterbacks, as Hartline and OC Tim Beck got Michael Van 
Buren by way of Mississippi State and LSU and Luke Kromenhoek 
by way of Florida State and Mississippi State. MVB did have some 
success at those two stops, including an 8/2 TD/INT ratio at LSU last 
season with four starts and some relief efforts. There are so many 
unproven players on this side of the ball and it’s fair to wonder if 
Hartline is a program-builder or was just able to thrive with the 
foundation already set at Ohio State.
What the Beck?
You can understand why Hartline turned to Tim Beck as the OC, as 
the 60-year-old has been coaching since the late ‘80s. It took him 35 
years to get his first head coaching gig and it didn’t go particularly 
well at Coastal Carolina with a 20-18 record. So, he’s an OC again 
and I find it underwhelming, personally. Most of the guys acquired 
via free agency didn’t play very much at their previous schools, but 
247Sports graded USF’s portal haul the best in the conference and 
58th nationally with 44 total commits. That’s a lot of scouting and a 
lot of new faces.
Could the defense outpace the offense in 2026?
While the hiring of Beck is pretty bland in my eyes, the hiring of 
Josh Aldridge as DC is not. Aldridge has been working at conference 
rival East Carolina under head coach Blake Harrell, who has proven 
to be an outstanding defensive mind and a pretty darn good HC. 
Stopping the run is the key to success in this conference. Most 
teams run the ball well or have run-heavy schemes. Aldridge’s ECU 
unit allowed just 3.6 yards per carry. Everybody seems to allow 
passing yards and 60+% completion percentages, but the teams that 
stop the run position themselves for success. That was true of USF 
last season with just 3.7 YPC. This may not be a polished defense, 
but it is a big front seven.

Who will lead Temple in 2026?
Evan Simon was a calming presence and a productive one for 
Temple, as he posted a 25/2 TD/INT ratio, leading the team to its 
first positive TO margin in quite some time. Before Keeler took 
over, Temple was -10, -20, and -11 in TO margin under Stan Drayton. 
Simon’s safe, reliable throws didn’t produce a ton of yardage, and 
he only had 19 TD passes after throwing six in the first game against 
UMass, but he protected the ball and gave the undermanned 
defense a better chance than his predecessors. With Simon and 
backup Gevani McCoy gone, there is virtually no experience on the 
roster, with Penn State’s Jaxon Smolik, who played in four games 
over three years at Penn State, and Ajani Sheppard, who played five 
games at Rutgers and zero last season at Washington State, as the 
primary QB options. It looks like a huge downturn is coming.
Where will the negative plays come from?
Temple only had 16 sacks last season and still allowed over six yards 
per play. While the defense shaved off nearly six PPG, it was really 
all about the turnover margin, as most of the per-play and rate stats 
weren’t really that much better under DC Brian Smith. The Owls 
had one of the worst red-zone defenses in the nation, were below 
the national average in third-down defense, and allowed 30 plays 
of 30+ yards. There are more returnees on offense than defense, so 
Smith has a lot of work to do. While three of the top four tacklers 
are back, the team’s leaders in pass breakups and sacks are not 
among them.
Will the real Temple Owls please stand up?
Temple finished the season -624 in yards, but they had some wild 
swings. The Owls outgained UMass by 165 yards, Howard by 439, 
and Navy by 134. On the flip side, they were outgained by 411 yards 
by Oklahoma, 140 by Georgia Tech, 381 by East Carolina, 202 by 
Tulane, and 289 by North Texas. In other words, over their last four 
games, even outgaining Army, they were -854 yards (while being 
+1 in TO margin!). That speaks to a major depth issue late in the 
season, something that Keeler and his staff have possibly addressed. 
The top of the American doesn’t seem as strong this season, but the 
conference as a whole seems better than it was last year, so Temple 
may have closer games to navigate.

Will Hall experience the regression Sumrall did not?
Tulane’s 11-3 record certainly stands out, but let’s look deeper, 
shall we? The Green Wave only outscored opponents 27.7-23.9 and 
only outgained them by a half-yard per play, with that discrepancy 
largely coming from a +24 sack differential. Tulane won four games 
in which they were outgained and five games by one score. Some 
of that may have been Sumrall and his late-game coaching in close 
contests. Some of that may have been luck. Some of that may have 
been Retzlaff, who led the team in rushing and had 16 rushing 
scores. But, it sure feels like it could all come crashing down on 
Hall, who was an awful head coach at Southern Miss and doesn’t 
have nearly the offensive upside of last year’s squad.
Who are the impact players on offense?
The fact that Retzlaff was available was truly a gift for Tulane 
because they were not set up well at the running back position with 
Makhi Hughes’ transfer. Jamauri McClure had 6.5 yards per carry on 
just 83 attempts and Javin Gordon only had 4.0 YPC on 128 attempts. 
Shazz Preston was the leading receiver by 200 yards and he’s gone, 
leaving behind second-leading WR Anthony Brown-Stevenson, who 
only had two fewer catches than Preston. Zeon Chriss-Gremillion 
has played like 12 years of college football and the only notable 
thing is that he’s got a hyphenated last name now. Kadin Semonza 
was there last year, but redshirted and didn’t play at all after starting 
for Ball State. So the answer to that question is that we don’t know.
Is the defense going to bail out the offense?
Tulane’s portal class ranks seventh in the 14-team American 
Conference, so that’s not terribly impressive given that they’ve had 
three seasons of 11+ wins and another 9-5 campaign over the last 
four years. Promoting Tayler Polk to full-fledged DC as opposed to 
co-DC may have helped keep leading tacklers Jack Tchienchou and 
Chris Rodgers around. That said, this was a defense that struggled 
against the pass last season, giving up 262 yards per game and a 
67.6% completion rate. Most of the 25 takeaways from last season 
are gone. Concerns run really deep on both sides of the ball.
